screens.title: Chaincode: Smart Contracts and Business Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode is the piece of code that encodes your business rules in Hyperledger Fabric. It governs how assets are created, read, updated, and deleted on a channel, and it runs inside an isolated environment on endorsing peers. In Fabric, execution and ordering are separated: endorsing peers simulate transactions and produce a read/write set, and the ordering service later sequences and commits those changes. This separation improves performance and helps preserve confidentiality. In practice, you will package your chaincode, install it on peers, have each organization approve its definition, and finally commit that definition so the chaincode becomes active on the channel. Writing chaincode requires careful attention: avoid non-deterministic logic, choose proper serialization, and consider private data collections for secrets. Over the next screens we will study the lifecycle steps, inspect a Go chaincode example with CreateAsset and ReadAsset, and practice deploying and interacting with a simple chaincode on the test-network. By the end, you will understand why lifecycle governance matters, how chaincode executes, and which common mistakes to avoid when designing business logic.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Chaincode Overview
Chaincode: Smart Contracts and Business Logic
Implement business rules that peers execute; governed and activated through a collaborative lifecycle.
What you will learn

Execution
Simulation
Ordering

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will be able to define chaincode and explain its role in enforcing business rules on a Fabric channel. You will understand the multi-step lifecycle that moves chaincode from source code to an active contract on a channel, including packaging, installation, approval by organizations, and commitment. You will develop a basic chaincode function in Go that reads from and writes to the ledger state, and you will identify common development pitfalls such as non-deterministic calls or improper error handling. Each objective is practical: defining chaincode clarifies where rules run; understanding lifecycle steps helps you manage governance and upgrades; implementing simple Go functions prepares you for real deployments; and spotting pitfalls prevents consensus and security failures. These outcomes are tied to hands-on actions like packaging a chaincode tarball, invoking CreateAsset, and using GetState and PutState safely. As you progress, verify competency by running the lifecycle commands and successfully creating and reading an asset on the test-network.

screens.title: What is Chaincode?
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode is the name Fabric uses for smart contracts. More precisely, chaincode encapsulates the business rules that determine how assets and transactions behave on a channel. When a client application requests a transaction, endorsing peers run the chaincode in an isolated environment and simulate the transaction against their local state database. The result of that simulation is a read/write set and any returned payload, which the peer includes in a proposal response. Importantly, chaincode execution is separate from ordering and committing. This separation lets Fabric optimize performance and keep simulation confidential among endorsers. A concrete example is a simple asset contract that defines CreateAsset, ReadAsset, UpdateAsset, and DeleteAsset. Each function manipulates the ledger through PutState and GetState calls. A common misconception is that chaincode runs at commit time; it does not. It runs during the endorsement phase and must be deterministic so that all endorsers produce the same read/write set. The core takeaway: chaincode enforces rules, must be deterministic, and is governed by a collaborative lifecycle so participants agree on the code that will shape their shared ledger. What is Chaincode? means chaincode is fabric's smart contract layer that runs business logic on peers during the endorsement phase and produces the read/write set used to form transactions.. In practical terms, fabric's implementation of smart contracts that encodes business logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Chaincode is Fabric's smart contract layer that runs business logic on peers during the endorsement phase and produces the read/write set used to form transactions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is Chaincode?
Chaincode defined
Chaincode packages the business rules that peers execute to validate and propose state changes. It uses the PutState and GetState APIs to interact with the ledger's state database.
Analogy
Think of chaincode as the contract script that every authorized participant reads and runs to agree how an asset should behave.
Concrete example
A CreateAsset function accepts asset fields, marshals them to JSON, and calls PutState with an ID key to persist the asset.
Misconception
Chaincode does not run during ordering or commit; it runs earlier during endorsement and must be deterministic across peers.
How chaincode interacts
Endorsing peers execute chaincode against their local state. The chaincode produces a read/write set that is then sent back to the client and later ordered and committed by the ordering service.
Example function list
  • CreateAsset — marshal fields and PutState
  • ReadAsset — GetState and return JSON
  • UpdateAsset — modify fields then PutState
  • DeleteAsset — remove key using DelState
Key Takeaway

Chaincode enforces deterministic business logic during endorsement; design functions to be serializable and free of external, variable inputs.

screens.title: Chaincode Lifecycle Overview
screens.narratorSegment: The chaincode lifecycle is a deliberately collaborative sequence that ensures organizations agree on the exact code and policies before it becomes active on a channel. The four canonical phases are package, install, approve for my organization, and commit. Packaging bundles the source into a tarball with a descriptor so peers can later identify the chaincode. Installation places that package on the peer file system and makes it available for execution, but not yet active. Each organization must then submit an approval transaction that records the chaincode definition metadata for that organization — this includes name, version, sequence, and the endorsement policy. The approvals are recorded on the channel and can be queried to check commit readiness. Finally, when a sufficient set of approvals exists, one organization submits a commit transaction to the ordering service. A successful commit makes the chaincode definition active and peers can begin endorsing transactions for that chaincode. This lifecycle enforces decentralized governance so no single organization can unilaterally change a shared contract. Chaincode Lifecycle Overview means the lifecycle is a four-step governance process that packages code, installs it on peers, collects per-organization approvals, and commits the definition to activate chaincode.. In practical terms, pack, install, approve, and commit — governance for chaincode activation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: The lifecycle is a four-step governance process that packages code, installs it on peers, collects per-organization approvals, and commits the definition to activate chaincode.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Lifecycle Overview
1
Package
Bundle source and descriptor into a tar.gz so installations reference the same code package.
2
Install
Install the package on endorsing peers' file systems to make the code available for simulation.
3
Approve for my organization
Submit an approval transaction that records your organization's acceptance of the chaincode definition and its endorsement policy.
4
Commit
Once the required organizations have approved, submit a commit transaction to the ordering service to activate the chaincode.
Practical checks
  • After install, use queryinstalled to obtain the package ID.
  • Use checkcommitreadiness to confirm enough approvals exist before commit.
  • Commit will make the chaincode available for endorsement and execution.
Key Takeaway

Lifecycle acts as governance: each organization must explicitly approve the chaincode definition before it is committed and activated.

screens.title: Packaging and Installation Details
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging creates a tarball that contains the chaincode source and a small descriptor so peers and tools can identify the package. The package step is deterministic: everyone must package the same source and metadata so installations refer to the same logical code. After packaging, the peer lifecycle install command places the package on the peer's file system and returns information that lets you query installed packages to find the package ID. That package ID is required in the subsequent approve step. A concrete command from the test-network example packages a chaincode directory into a tar. gz using peer lifecycle chaincode package with the path, language, and label. After installation, peer lifecycle chaincode queryinstalled will print the package ID, which looks like a label followed by a hash. One common pitfall is using different package labels or modifying code after packaging without updating the sequence and approvals. Always package once from the final source and share the package ID with operational teams to ensure consistent approvals. Packaging and Installation Details means package from the final source and record the package id after queryinstalled; mismatched packages cause approval mismatches.. In practical terms, how to create a package and install it on peers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Packaging & Install
Packaging
Use the peer lifecycle chaincode package command to create a tar.gz that includes source and a descriptor. The label you choose helps identify the package but the package ID includes a content hash.
Example command
peer lifecycle chaincode package simple_chaincode.tar.gz --path ../chaincode/simple_chaincode --lang golang --label simple_chaincode_v1
After installation, queryinstalled returns the package ID string that you will export as CC_PACKAGE_ID for approveformyorg. Keep that identifier unchanged throughout approval and commit steps.
Installation and Query
Install the package on an endorsing peer. Installing makes the code available for simulation but does not activate it on a channel.
Install example
peer lifecycle chaincode install simple_chaincode.tar.gz
peer lifecycle chaincode queryinstalled
Key Takeaway

The package ID from queryinstalled is required for approval; treat it as a stable reference when managing approvals and commits.

screens.title: Approval and Commit: Governance in Action
screens.narratorSegment: After install, each organization that will endorse transactions must explicitly approve the chaincode definition for their org. Approving records the organization's acceptance of metadata such as the chaincode name, version, sequence, and the endorsement policy. Approval is submitted as a transaction to the ordering service; it does not by itself activate the chaincode. Instead, the approvals are visible on the channel and you can run checkcommitreadiness to see which organizations have approved. Only once the required set of organizations have approved will a commit transaction succeed in making the chaincode definition active. A practical example: export the package ID obtained from queryinstalled, then run peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg with channel, name, version, sequence, and init-required flags. Then use checkcommitreadiness with the same parameters to confirm. If readiness indicates the necessary approvals are present, submit the commit transaction with commitchanneldefinition or commit commands that include peer addresses. This collaborative process prevents unilateral changes and preserves trust. Approval and Commit: Governance in Action means each org must approve the chaincode definition; commit only after checkcommitreadiness confirms the required approvals.. In practical terms, approve for my organization and commit when readiness is satisfied. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Each org must approve the chaincode definition; commit only after checkcommitreadiness confirms the required approvals.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Approve & Commit
Approve for my organization
Use the package ID and submit approveformyorg with the channel ID, name, version, sequence, and required flags. This transaction records your organization's approval on the channel ledger.
Approve example
export CC_PACKAGE_ID="YOUR_PACKAGE_ID_HERE"
peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg -o localhost:7050 --tls --cafile ... --channelID mychannel --name simple_chaincode --version 1.0 --package-id $CC_PACKAGE_ID --sequence 1 --init-required --waitForEvent
Check readiness and commit
Run checkcommitreadiness to confirm needed approvals. If readiness is satisfied, submit the commit transaction that activates the chaincode definition on the channel.
Check and commit
peer lifecycle chaincode checkcommitreadiness --channelID mychannel --name simple_chaincode --version 1.0 --sequence 1 --init-required --output json
# after approvals
peer lifecycle chaincode commitchanneldefinition -o localhost:7050 --tls --cafile ... --channelID mychannel --name simple_chaincode --version 1.0 --sequence 1 --init-required --peerAddresses localhost:7051 --tlsRootCertFiles ...
Key Takeaway

Approvals record organizational consent; commit only after readiness checks to ensure the chaincode definition is agreed upon.

screens.title: Init and Invoke in Go Chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: Two functions are central in a basic Go chaincode: Init and Invoke. Init is called during instantiation or upgrade and typically performs initialization tasks such as setting up default state. Invoke is called for every transaction and dispatches to specific business logic functions based on the requested function name. A standard pattern is to call stub. GetFunctionAndParameters to obtain the function name and args, then route to CreateAsset, ReadAsset, UpdateAsset, or other handlers. Keep Init minimal and deterministic: it should not perform external calls or randomized behavior. Similarly, Invoke should parse inputs carefully, validate argument counts, and return clear errors when input validation fails. Below is a readable excerpt of the Init and Invoke functions from the example. Note how Invoke prints the function name for audit, checks which function was called, and returns shim. Error for an invalid name. Always validate inputs early to prevent malformed state writes and to keep simulations deterministic across endorsers. Init and Invoke in Go Chaincode means init handles setup at instantiation; invoke routes transactions to business functions and must validate inputs and keep execution deterministic.. In practical terms, understanding initialization and transaction dispatch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Init vs Invoke
keyIdea.text: Init handles setup at instantiation; Invoke routes transactions to business functions and must validate inputs and keep execution deterministic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Init & Invoke
Code excerpt (Init & Invoke)
// Init is called during chaincode instantiation or upgrade
func (t *SimpleChaincode) Init(stub shim.ChaincodeStubInterface) peer.Response {
  fmt.Println("Chaincode Initialized")
  return shim.Success(nil)
}

// Invoke is called for every transaction
func (t *SimpleChaincode) Invoke(stub shim.ChaincodeStubInterface) peer.Response {
  function, args := stub.GetFunctionAndParameters()
  fmt.Printf("Invoke called, function: %s, args: %v
", function, args)

  if function == "CreateAsset" {
    return t.CreateAsset(stub, args)
  } else if function == "ReadAsset" {
    return t.ReadAsset(stub, args)
  }

  return shim.Error("Invalid chaincode function name. Expecting 'CreateAsset' or 'ReadAsset'")
}
  • Init should be deterministic and minimal — avoid external resources.
  • Invoke must parse function names and validate the argument count before calling handlers.
  • Return meaningful errors to help diagnose failed simulations that cause endorsement mismatches.
Common mistakes
Not validating args length, performing non-deterministic operations, and doing external network calls inside Init or Invoke can break consensus.
Key Takeaway

Keep Init and Invoke simple, deterministic, and fully validated so endorsers produce identical read/write sets for the same inputs.

screens.title: CreateAsset and ReadAsset Explained
screens.narratorSegment: CreateAsset and ReadAsset are concrete examples of CRUD operations against the ledger state. CreateAsset typically validates argument count, constructs an asset struct, marshals it to JSON, and calls PutState with a chosen key. A critical implementation detail is correct JSON marshaling and error handling: always check for errors when marshaling and when calling PutState. ReadAsset fetches data using GetState, checks for nil results to detect missing assets, and returns the stored bytes as the response. In the provided Go example, asset fields like ID, color, size, owner, and value are marshaled and stored under the asset ID key. A common mistake is mismatching expected argument counts, which can cause runtime errors or incorrect state. Another trap is converting string arguments to integers incorrectly — validate conversions and return informative errors. Finally, never store sensitive information directly on the ledger; use private data collections for confidentiality. The practical lesson: validate, marshal, store, and always return clear errors so simulations remain predictable and diagnosable. In practical terms, how to model assets and use putstate/getstate safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Create & Read
CreateAsset code (excerpt)
CreateAsset validates argument count, builds the asset struct, marshals to JSON, and calls PutState. Errors are returned as shim.Error to signal failed simulation.
// CreateAsset creates a new asset
func (t *SimpleChaincode) CreateAsset(stub shim.ChaincodeStubInterface, args []string) peer.Response {
  if len(args) != 5 {
    return shim.Error("Incorrect number of arguments. Expecting 5 for CreateAsset.")
  }

  asset := Asset{
    ID:    args[0],
    Color: args[1],
    Size:  json.Number(args[2]).Int64(),
    Owner: args[3],
    Value: json.Number(args[4]).Int64(),
  }

  assetAsBytes, err := json.Marshal(asset)
  if err != nil {
    return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Failed to marshal asset: %s", err))
  }

  err = stub.PutState(asset.ID, assetAsBytes)
  if err != nil {
    return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Failed to create asset: %s", err))
  }

  return shim.Success(assetAsBytes)
}
ReadAsset code (excerpt)
// ReadAsset reads an asset from the ledger
func (t *SimpleChaincode) ReadAsset(stub shim.ChaincodeStubInterface, args []string) peer.Response {
  if len(args) != 1 {
    return shim.Error("Incorrect number of arguments. Expecting 1 for ReadAsset.")
  }

  assetID := args[0]
  assetAsBytes, err := stub.GetState(assetID)
  if err != nil {
    return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Failed to read asset: %s", err))
  }
  if assetAsBytes == nil {
    return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Asset with ID %s does not exist", assetID))
  }

  return shim.Success(assetAsBytes)
}
Key Takeaway

Always validate args and conversions, marshal reliably, and return explicit errors so endorsers produce the same read/write set.

screens.title: Deterministic vs Non-deterministic Chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: Determinism means that when the same function is executed with the same inputs, every endorsing peer produces the same read/write set. Fabric requires deterministic chaincode so the ledger state remains consistent after ordering and commit. Non-deterministic operations include calls to random number generators, access to system time without careful handling, or external network calls that can return different data on different peers. If chaincode used a random number to set an asset value, different endorsers could propose different write sets and consensus would fail. To avoid this, keep chaincode pure with respect to inputs: any required randomness or external data should be provided by the client as part of the transaction input and validated by the chaincode. Use private data collections for confidential inputs rather than embedding secrets in the chaincode state visible to all channel peers. The practical guideline is simple: deterministic functions, explicit inputs, and careful modeling of private data preserve consensus and confidentiality. Deterministic chaincode
Produces the same read/write set on every endorsing peer when given the same inputs. This is required for ledger consistency.
Correct pattern
Accept external data as transaction inputs from the client and validate them deterministically inside chaincode.
Incorrect pattern
Call random number generators, system time, or external services directly from chaincode during endorsement.
Example pitfall
If CreateAsset uses a runtime random value for the asset's value field, different endorsers may write different values, making the transaction invalid across the network.
Pro Tip

When deterministic random-like values are required, have the client produce them and include them as transaction args, then chaincode can validate a signature or checksum to avoid drift.

screens.title: Endorsing Peers and Execution Model
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric separates concerns: endorsing peers execute chaincode to simulate transactions and produce read/write sets; the ordering service sequences transactions; and committing peers update the ledger. Endorsing peers do not commit the transaction when they simulate it — they only produce a proposal response. The client collects responses from endorsers, packages them into a transaction, and submits it to the ordering service. Ordering does not execute chaincode; it simply orders and packages transactions into blocks. Committing peers then validate the transaction, using the endorsement policy and MVCC checks, and write the state updates to the ledger. This architecture allows Fabric to support flexible endorsement policies, private data, and higher throughput because heavy execution work is done in parallel by endorsing peers and ordering is independent of execution. A misconception to avoid is thinking ordering runs chaincode; it does not. Understanding this separation helps you design endorsement policies that balance trust, performance, and confidentiality. Role of each component
Endorsing peers
Execute chaincode, simulate transactions against local state, produce read/write sets and proposal responses used for endorsement.
Ordering service
Sequences transactions into blocks but does not execute chaincode; it handles consistency of ordering across the channel.
Committing peers
Validate endorsement policy and multi-version concurrency control, then apply state updates to the ledger.
Practical implication
Because execution is separate, you can tune endorsement policies for trust and performance, and use private data for confidential state only visible to authorized peers.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Testing, Serialization, and Data Modeling
screens.narratorSegment: Good chaincode design emphasizes modular functions, clear serialization, and a state model that supports efficient queries. Break business logic into small, testable functions that you can run in unit tests without a live network. Use JSON for data interchange and keep schema stable so upgrades are manageable. When converting numeric strings to integers, validate conversions and return explicit errors to avoid panics during endorsement. Design keys thoughtfully: composite keys and namespaces help avoid collisions and make queries efficient. If you need confidentiality, use private data collections rather than writing secrets to the channel ledger. Also write unit tests to assert PutState and GetState behavior so you catch argument mismatches and type conversion issues early. A frequent mistake is storing large or unnecessary data on the ledger; prefer references or off-ledger storage for bulky content while keeping authoritative metadata on-chain. These practices make chaincode safer, easier to maintain, and less likely to produce endorsement mismatches in production. fullNarratorScript:
Chaincode is the piece of code that encodes your business rules in Hyperledger Fabric. It governs how assets are created, read, updated, and deleted on a channel, and it runs inside an isolated environment on endorsing peers. In Fabric, execution and ordering are separated: endorsing peers simulate transactions and produce a read/write set, and the ordering service later sequences and commits those changes. This separation improves performance and helps preserve confidentiality. In practice, you will package your chaincode, install it on peers, have each organization approve its definition, and finally commit that definition so the chaincode becomes active on the channel. Writing chaincode requires careful attention: avoid non-deterministic logic, choose proper serialization, and consider private data collections for secrets. Over the next screens we will study the lifecycle steps, inspect a Go chaincode example with CreateAsset and ReadAsset, and practice deploying and interacting with a simple chaincode on the test-network. By the end, you will understand why lifecycle governance matters, how chaincode executes, and which common mistakes to avoid when designing business logic.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to define chaincode and explain its role in enforcing business rules on a Fabric channel. You will understand the multi-step lifecycle that moves chaincode from source code to an active contract on a channel, including packaging, installation, approval by organizations, and commitment. You will develop a basic chaincode function in Go that reads from and writes to the ledger state, and you will identify common development pitfalls such as non-deterministic calls or improper error handling. Each objective is practical: defining chaincode clarifies where rules run; understanding lifecycle steps helps you manage governance and upgrades; implementing simple Go functions prepares you for real deployments; and spotting pitfalls prevents consensus and security failures. These outcomes are tied to hands-on actions like packaging a chaincode tarball, invoking CreateAsset, and using GetState and PutState safely. As you progress, verify competency by running the lifecycle commands and successfully creating and reading an asset on the test-network.

Practical verification matters. For each objective, you should be able to demonstrate a concrete action: describe chaincode and give an example of an asset contract; run the packaging and installation commands to produce a package ID; write and run a small Go function that creates an asset and returns the created value; and point out why a random number call breaks consensus. These demonstrations map directly to the lifecycle commands and code examples we'll show. A useful practice is to first implement functions that return deterministic, serializable outputs, then write unit tests that assert expected state changes. When you run the test-network example, the peer lifecycle commands will show package IDs and commit confirmations; your successful CreateAsset and ReadAsset calls will return the JSON asset. These checks prove both technical skill and an understanding of governance. Keep in mind the goal: your chaincode must be auditable, deterministic, and agreed upon by the organizations that will endorse transactions.

Chaincode is the name Fabric uses for smart contracts. More precisely, chaincode encapsulates the business rules that determine how assets and transactions behave on a channel. When a client application requests a transaction, endorsing peers run the chaincode in an isolated environment and simulate the transaction against their local state database. The result of that simulation is a read/write set and any returned payload, which the peer includes in a proposal response. Importantly, chaincode execution is separate from ordering and committing. This separation lets Fabric optimize performance and keep simulation confidential among endorsers. A concrete example is a simple asset contract that defines CreateAsset, ReadAsset, UpdateAsset, and DeleteAsset. Each function manipulates the ledger through PutState and GetState calls. A common misconception is that chaincode runs at commit time; it does not. It runs during the endorsement phase and must be deterministic so that all endorsers produce the same read/write set. The core takeaway: chaincode enforces rules, must be deterministic, and is governed by a collaborative lifecycle so participants agree on the code that will shape their shared ledger. What is Chaincode? means chaincode is fabric's smart contract layer that runs business logic on peers during the endorsement phase and produces the read/write set used to form transactions.. In practical terms, fabric's implementation of smart contracts that encodes business logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The chaincode lifecycle is a deliberately collaborative sequence that ensures organizations agree on the exact code and policies before it becomes active on a channel. The four canonical phases are package, install, approve for my organization, and commit. Packaging bundles the source into a tarball with a descriptor so peers can later identify the chaincode. Installation places that package on the peer file system and makes it available for execution, but not yet active. Each organization must then submit an approval transaction that records the chaincode definition metadata for that organization — this includes name, version, sequence, and the endorsement policy. The approvals are recorded on the channel and can be queried to check commit readiness. Finally, when a sufficient set of approvals exists, one organization submits a commit transaction to the ordering service. A successful commit makes the chaincode definition active and peers can begin endorsing transactions for that chaincode. This lifecycle enforces decentralized governance so no single organization can unilaterally change a shared contract. Chaincode Lifecycle Overview means the lifecycle is a four-step governance process that packages code, installs it on peers, collects per-organization approvals, and commits the definition to activate chaincode.. In practical terms, pack, install, approve, and commit — governance for chaincode activation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Packaging creates a tarball that contains the chaincode source and a small descriptor so peers and tools can identify the package. The package step is deterministic: everyone must package the same source and metadata so installations refer to the same logical code. After packaging, the peer lifecycle install command places the package on the peer's file system and returns information that lets you query installed packages to find the package ID. That package ID is required in the subsequent approve step. A concrete command from the test-network example packages a chaincode directory into a tar. gz using peer lifecycle chaincode package with the path, language, and label. After installation, peer lifecycle chaincode queryinstalled will print the package ID, which looks like a label followed by a hash. One common pitfall is using different package labels or modifying code after packaging without updating the sequence and approvals. Determinism means that when the same function is executed with the same inputs, every endorsing peer produces the same read/write set. Fabric requires deterministic chaincode so the ledger state remains consistent after ordering and commit. Non-deterministic operations include calls to random number generators, access to system time without careful handling, or external network calls that can return different data on different peers. If chaincode used a random number to set an asset value, different endorsers could propose different write sets and consensus would fail. To avoid this, keep chaincode pure with respect to inputs: any required randomness or external data should be provided by the client as part of the transaction input and validated by the chaincode. Use private data collections for confidential inputs rather than embedding secrets in the chaincode state visible to all channel peers. Fabric separates concerns: endorsing peers execute chaincode to simulate transactions and produce read/write sets; the ordering service sequences transactions; and committing peers update the ledger. Endorsing peers do not commit the transaction when they simulate it — they only produce a proposal response. The client collects responses from endorsers, packages them into a transaction, and submits it to the ordering service. Ordering does not execute chaincode; it simply orders and packages transactions into blocks. Committing peers then validate the transaction, using the endorsement policy and MVCC checks, and write the state updates to the ledger. This architecture allows Fabric to support flexible endorsement policies, private data, and higher throughput because heavy execution work is done in parallel by endorsing peers and ordering is independent of execution. A misconception to avoid is thinking ordering runs chaincode; it does not. Understanding this separation helps you design endorsement policies that balance trust, performance, and confidentiality.
